title: Orbital-Selective Mott and Antiferromagnetic Phases in Diagonally Compressed Kagome Lattice
authors: Jiewei Ding, Ho-Kin Tang, Wing Chi Yu
abstract: We perform determinant quantum Monte Carlo simulations of the half-filled Hubbard model on a diagonally compressed kagome lattice, introducing exponential decay long-range hopping $t(r) = t_0 \exp\bigl(-r / r_0\bigr)$ to account for the evolving bond length. By varying the lattice angle $θ$ and the on-site interaction $U$, double occupancy, charge compressibility, and spin-spin correlation functions of the whole system and each sub-lattice are measured. We find that geometric compression induces a clear sublattice differentiation: for $θ\gtrsim52^\circ$, the A sublattice establishes long-range hoppings, which in turn suppresses the metallic behavior of the $B/C$ sublattice and drives a selective Mott transition; for $θ\lesssim52^\circ$, the $B$-$C$ chains develop long-range antiferromagnetic correlations within the finite-size simulations, which in turn suppresses the metallic behavior of the $A$ sublattice and drives a selective Mott transition. The critical interaction $U^c_A$ for the $A$ sites decreases sharply near the onset of $B$-$C$ antiferromagnetic correlations, while $U^c_{B/C}$ increases. These competing orders give rise to an orbital-selective Mott phase and a rich $U$-$θ$ phase diagram featuring paramagnetic-metal, paramagnetic-Mott, antiferromagnetic-metal, and antiferromagnetic-Mott states. Our results highlight the complex interplay between lattice geometry, magnetic frustration, and strong correlations in frustrated two-dimensional systems.
summary: This work uses Quantum Monte Carlo simulations to study a Hubbard model on a compressed Kagome lattice. By varying the lattice angle $\theta$, the authors demonstrate that geometric changes induce sublattice differentiation, leading to an orbital-selective Mott phase. This highlights how geometry can compete with magnetic frustration to dictate the electronic ground state in strongly correlated materials.
main_problem: The study investigates the complex interplay between lattice geometry, magnetic frustration, and strong electronic correlations in two-dimensional systems.
main_result: Geometric compression induces sublattice differentiation, leading to an orbital-selective Mott phase and a rich U-theta phase diagram featuring multiple distinct metallic and Mott insulating states.
method: The research employs Determinant Quantum Monte Carlo (DQMC) simulations on the half-filled Hubbard model.
model_or_system: The system is modeled by the Hubbard Hamiltonian on a diagonally compressed Kagome lattice, incorporating long-range hopping via an exponential decay function $t(r)$.
key_observables: Double occupancy, charge compressibility ($\kappa$), spin-spin correlation functions ($G_z(r), G_x(r)$), and sublattice charge responses.
important_parameters: Lattice angle $\theta$ (compression parameter) and on-site interaction $U$.
main_assumptions: The hopping amplitude is modeled by an exponential decay, and the analysis relies on interpreting the low-temperature behavior of compressibility to determine charge gaps.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the lattice geometry changes with $\theta$, the evolution of hopping strengths between sublattices A, B, and C, and plots showing how compressibility ($\ln \kappa$ vs $1/T$) reveals insulating behavior at different angles.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the system by varying the compression angle $\theta$ and interaction strength $U$, using DQMC to map out a phase diagram characterized by distinct electronic and magnetic orders (PM-metal, AFM-Mott, etc.).
why_interesting: While focused on lattice geometry rather than direct AMO platforms, the concept of tuning interactions and correlations via engineered hopping anisotropy is highly relevant for designing quantum simulators using ultracold atoms or superconducting circuits.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. (a) Schematic of the kagome lattice before and af- ter compression. Solid lines indicate fixed AB and AC bond lengths; the dashed line shows the BC bond shortening as the angle θ decreases. (b) Exponential decay of hopping strength t(r) with distance r. (c) Evolution of the lattice geometry with θ. (d) and (e): Hopping amplitudes between sublattices A and B and their 10 nearest sites, with line thickness pro- portional to t.

FIG. 2. Average sign ⟨s⟩at the lowest temperature T = 0.5 as a function of the compression angle θ along the half-filling line. Different curves correspond to different values of U. For each (U, θ), the chemical potential is fixed by the half- filling condition n = 1. Error bars denote the standard error estimated from independent Monte Carlo simulations.

FIG. 3. Band structures of the diagonally compressed kagome lattice in the non-interacting limit for θ = 60◦, 54◦, and 46◦, obtained by diagonalizing the 3 × 3 Bloch Hamiltonian with the same distance-dependent hopping used in the DQMC sim- ulations at U = 0 and µ = 0. Energies are measured in units of the nearest-neighbor hopping t with r = 0.5 of the undis- torted lattice. As θ decreases, the enhanced BC hopping ren- ders the kagome flat band dispersive and increases the overall bandwidth.

FIG. 4. Temperature dependence of the global chemical po- tential µh required to impose half filling (n = 1) for various interaction strengths U. Panels (a-c) show µh(T) for different lattice angles θ. Error bars indicate the standard error esti- mated from ten independent Monte Carlo simulations.

FIG. 5. Temperature dependence of the average particle num- ber on sublattice A and sublattices B/C when the system is at half-filling. Error bars represent the standard error esti- mated from ten independent Monte Carlo simulations.
